title: Objects, arrays and references
idea: Objects, arrays and functions are stored by reference: a variable holds a link to the object, so two variables can share and change the same one.

analogy.text: A shared document link. Two people hold the same link, so an edit by one shows for the other. Sending the link copies the link, not the document.
analogy.breaks: Real links can go dead; a JavaScript reference never dangles.

points: Objects, arrays and functions live on the heap; variables hold a reference to them.
Assigning `b = a` copies the reference, so both names reach one object.
`===` on objects asks whether both sides are the same object, not equal contents.
Spread `{ ...a }` copies one level; `structuredClone(a)` copies nested objects too.

steps.caption: Line 1 creates an object on the heap. The variable `a` holds a reference to it.
Line 2 copies the reference, not the object. `a` and `b` now point at the same object.
Line 3 changes the object through `b`. There is only one object, so `a` sees the change.
Line 4 spreads `a` into a new object. `c` gets its own object with copied values.
Line 5 changes the copy only. The first object is untouched.
Line 6 reads through two different references to two different objects.

code.title: Alias, spread, structuredClone
code.caption: Run it. Then push to `copy.tags` and see which lengths change.

pitfalls: Spread is shallow: nested objects stay shared. Use `structuredClone` for a deep copy.
Do not use `===` to compare contents; compare the fields you need.
`structuredClone` throws on functions, so clone plain data only.

quiz.why: `q` is an alias, so `p.n` becomes 9 and `p === q`. `r` is a new object, so `p === r` is false.

takeaway: Variables hold references; assigning copies the link, not the object.

starters: Why does changing one variable change another?
